title: Lughaidh finds a new-cut stone in the western grass
summary: Driving his flock further west than his own hearth has grazed before, the shepherd Lughaidh comes on a standing stone raised so lately that the turned earth at its foot has not yet greened over, with no camp, path or tool-litter left by whatever hand set it there.

title: Two hands on one stone
summary: Lughaidh reads a line of unfamiliar script on the stone's upper face, cut broad and level by one hand, and below it four words of his own tongue, Bha teine sa chloich, cut narrower and shallower by another; neither hand has left any other mark on the hillside.

title: Lughaidh's find carried hearth to hearth
summary: The tale of the new stone in the western grass passes from Lughaidh's own hearth to the next and on beyond it, the four words kept exact in every mouth that takes them up while the stone's own size and the manner of its finding grow with the telling.

title: Clann na Ceiste claims the fire, and leaves the older line unread
summary: Word of the stone's four words reaches Tobar dhìreach, and the line holds the fire they name for its own, Teine a' Chlachair, while the broader script above them goes on unread, no eye at the line or beyond it able to say what hand cut it or when.

title: A second stone found in the stony hills
summary: A traveller crossing poor, broken ground further into the hills all but walks into a shorter stone before he sees it, and carries down word of three more words cut low upon it, Cuimhnich an teine, in what looks the same sure hand as the first stone's saying.

title: The line answers for a bidding cut to no one
summary: Asked by travellers whether the second stone's plain command speaks to them any clearer than the first, Clann na Ceiste answers each time the same: that the fire is theirs to remember whether the stone bade them or not, there being no other hand on the island that has minded it so long.

title: Lughaidh dies at his own hearth
summary: Lughaidh dies in his own seventieth year, remembered by his own valley chiefly as the shepherd who first said the stone's four words aloud on the hillside where they stand.

title: The four words said standing at the gathering
summary: At that year's gathering a young man of the line says Bha teine sa chloich aloud, standing, before the whole crowd for what the tellers hold to be the first time, the saying having come to him by the same slow road as every other hearth, from mouth to mouth, back to a shepherd fifty years gone.

title: Mòrnait born at Tobar dhìreach
summary: Mòrnait is born into a household gathered about Clann na Ceiste's own hearth without ever holding its coals, and grows up on Aithris a' Chruthachaidh and the two new sayings both, already part of the ordinary stock of what every child of the valleys knows by then.

title: Mòrnait carries fire to the second stone
summary: Mòrnait makes the hard day's walk into the stony hills with a coal from the line's own pot wrapped close against the wet, and builds at the foot of Colbh Cnoc chiar a ring of fire-cracked stones in which she lights and keeps a hearth-sized fire.

title: The ring at the pillar is kept and grows a path
summary: Mòrnait returns to the ring at Colbh Cnoc chiar year on year, joined in time by others who come to sit an evening by the fire before going their own ways, until a worn path runs to it across the broken ground and the ash within the stones lies black and deep.

title: Mòrnait holds the fire is kept, not questioned
summary: Asked more than once whether her fire is some new trial of the old riddle, Mòrnait answers that the stone asked only to be remembered, not questioned, there being questioning enough already given the two dark coals by better keepers than herself.

title: Mòrnait's last walk to the ring
summary: In her sixty-fifth year Mòrnait makes the walk to Colbh Cnoc chiar for the last time, and tells the few who sit with her that evening she does not know what the stone remembers, only that she has kept it as well as she knew how.

title: Mòrnait dies, and her daughter takes up the keeping
summary: Mòrnait dies at her own hearth some weeks after her last walk, and her daughter, and after her the daughter's own children, take up the walk to the ring in her stead, less often than Mòrnait kept it but often enough that the fire does not go cold.
